body:
### Summary

Currently, there seems to be no way to verify that a uv.lock has not maliciously been tampered with. It would be nice if this can be automatically checked, because manually verifying lock file changes is error-prone and likely often neglected (even the github UI hides uv.lock diffs per default).

I would like to have a command (part of `uv sync`, `uv lock` or `uv audit`) that checks if the dependencies in uv.lock match the definitions in pyproject.toml. I think this would require fetching the metadata again from PyPi.

This is to prevent against this scenario:
- some creates a malicious PR: pyproject.toml looks good (only pytest is updated); uv.lock has legitimate updates + a single wheel url has been changed to point to the attacker-controlled domain pythonhcsted instead of pythonhosted
- maintainer looks at the PR:
- - either only verifies the pyproject.toml diff. Easy and short to verify
- - or even expands the uv.lock diff and needs a lot of luck to find the difference between `pythonhcsted` and `pythonhosted` (`c` vs `o`)

It seems that the only safe way to handle PRs that add lines to uv.lock files is to close them, because I have no way to tell if there is a security issue hidden inside. I'd like that to be different, and also I guess many maintainers are not aware of this.

This issue is not unique to uv. For instance, here is an article describing malicious package-lock.json changes in npm: https://snyk.io/blog/why-npm-lockfiles-can-be-a-security-blindspot-for-injecting-malicious-modules/

### Example

I lack the knowledge how exactly things work in the background, but from a high level point of view I want something like this:

```bash
uv lock --verify
# check that there are no unexpected dependencies in `uv.lock` that are neither declared in pyproject.toml nor are they transitive dependencies
# verify that uv.lock versions are within the version ranges of pyproject.toml
# verify that sdist and wheel urls point to the urls described by the index in pyproject.toml
```

This could also be considered as a flag in setup-uv, so open source repositories are more likely to use this in their workflows before installing dependencies.
title: Command to verify uv.lock is legitimate
